narrative: Most brokers are reactive. They post the listing, run an email blast, and wait for the phone to ring. We do all of that, and we do it well. Then we do the part almost nobody does. We pick up the phone.

Before your building goes to market, our system builds a probable buyer list for it specifically. It pulls the county assessment record for every property in the surrounding area: who owns it, where their mail goes, what they paid, when they bought, who financed it, and how many other buildings they hold. Out of that come the three groups most likely to buy your building: owners of comparable product nearby, buyers who have closed on buildings like yours recently, and exchange buyers with money that has to be placed on a deadline.
That list runs well over 100 names, and we call every one of them.

overview: Newhall Terrace Apartments is a 66-unit apartment building at 24377 Newhall Avenue in Santa Clarita, built in 1972 on a 2.14 acre parcel and containing approximately 36,908 gross square feet across two stories.

The property is a single floor plan asset. All 66 units are one bedroom, one bath homes of approximately 550 square feet, which makes the rent roll unusually simple to underwrite and unusually simple to manage: one unit type, one turn cost, one market rent to solve for.

Rents in place average $1,583 per month. The market rent carried in the analysis is $1,950. Applied across all 66 units, that gap is roughly $290,000 of annual scheduled rent that the property is not currently collecting, and no entitlement, construction, or repositioning is required to reach it.

Because Santa Clarita has no local rent stabilization ordinance, the gap closes on turnover rather than through a capped annual increase. Seven units were vacant at the rent roll date, which means a portion of that repositioning is available to a buyer immediately rather than over a holding period.
properties.location_title: Walking Distance to Metrolink in Old Town Newhall
location_narrative: The property sits on Newhall Avenue at the edge of Old Town Newhall. Newhall Metrolink Station is three tenths of a mile away, a six minute walk, putting a tenant on a one seat rail ride to Burbank, Glendale, and Union Station without a car. The Oaks Plaza is two tenths of a mile from the door and the Newhall Crossings retail and residential development is three tenths of a mile.
William S. Hart Regional Park is a twelve minute walk. College of the Canyons is 4.8 miles out and Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital, one of the valley's largest employers, is 1.9 miles away.

This is the walkable end of the Santa Clarita Valley, which is uncommon in a market built overwhelmingly around the car. For a building of 550 square foot one bedrooms, a tenant base that can live here without a second vehicle is not a soft amenity, it is what supports the rent.
physical_narrative: Two stories, 66 units, approximately 36,908 gross square feet on a 93,152 square foot lot. The Los Angeles County Assessor records the property under APN 2830-017-015 as a Multi-Family Residence built in 1972, and the unit count, year built, building area, and lot size in this analysis all tie to that record.
Improvements sit across garden-style wings with on-site surface parking and on-site laundry facilities. Every unit has air conditioning and heating.
At 2.14 acres the parcel is generously sized for 66 units, roughly 31 units to the acre, with meaningful open and landscaped area rather than a building built to its lot lines.

The site is a single legal parcel assembled from lots 29, 30, 31 and 32 of Tract 1059 together with the adjoining vacated street, held in fee simple. It fronts Newhall Avenue between 9th Street and Chestnut Street.
market_narrative: Newhall is trading. Eight apartment properties in and around this submarket have closed or gone under contract since May 2025, including a four-property portfolio that changed hands in a single June 2026 transaction. Buyer demand here is real and it is currently deeper than the supply of listed product.

That demand is disciplined, not indiscriminate. An eight-unit building a fifth of a mile away has been marketed for eleven months without selling, at an ask well above where this submarket has actually been closing. Buyers here are active, and they are also willing to wait out a number they do not believe.
positioning_narrative: A 66-unit building is a different product from the seven and nine unit trades that make up most of this submarket's transaction count. It is large enough to carry professional management and to matter to a buyer who wants scale in one location, and small enough to clear with private capital or a single 1031 exchange rather than requiring an institution. That combination is scarce in the Santa Clarita Valley, and it is the core of the positioning.
rent_narrative: Nearby leased and asking rents are shown as a market sensitivity for the one bedroom floor plan and are not represented as achieved subject rents.
valuation_narrative: The recommendation is built on current income rather than on the pro forma. Closed arm's-length sales in Newhall run from $176,607 to $209,091 per unit, and the only closed trade at comparable scale, a 65-unit building half a mile up the same street, allocated at $182,692 per unit inside a four-property portfolio transaction.

On a per unit basis the recommendation sits at the upper end of that closed range, and on income it does not. The one closed sale in the set carrying a confirmed cap rate traded at 5.42%, and the escrow half a mile away is at 5.31%. The recommended value prices this property in line with both while its gross rent multiplier stays below every income-supported comparable in the analysis.

Two things move this number more than the comparables do. The first is the rent gap: 23% of upside on a building with no local rent control is what justifies pricing at the top of the per unit range rather than the middle. The second is expense underwriting. Repairs and management are carried at underwritten figures rather than the amounts on the owner's most recent operating summary, and a buyer who underwrites to those actuals will arrive at a lower net operating income. The sensitivity table shows that case explicitly.

The property was originally developed with 1987 low-income housing tax credits. That allocation carried a fifteen-year compliance period and no extended-use covenant, since the thirty-year requirement arrived only for allocations after 1989, and the restrictions expired in 2002. Ownership confirms the property carries no rent restriction and no age restriction today. Third-party data services still display the historical allocation, which is a record of a 1987 program rather than a live covenant. It does explain the rent profile: rents were held down for fifteen years and were never reset to market afterward.

Stabilized at market rent with utility bill-back in place, net operating income reaches $1,049,546. That figure is a projection of what the property can earn, not what it earns today, and it is not the basis of the recommendation.

strategy.title: Lead With the Rent Gap, Not the Vacancy
strategy.copy: The single most valuable fact about this property is that in-place rents sit roughly 23% below where the one-bedroom market is. A buyer does not have to renovate, re-entitle, or reposition anything to capture that. They have to hold the asset and re-lease units as they turn. That is the cleanest story in this submarket and it is what the campaign leads with.

buyer_profiles.title: The Valley Apartment Owner Adding Scale
buyer_profiles.copy: An owner who already holds 20 to 60 units across several Santa Clarita buildings and wants that same count under one roof, one manager, and one roof line. This is the buyer the assessment-record call list is built to find.

buyer_profiles.title: The 1031 Exchange Buyer on a Clock
buyer_profiles.copy: Exchange money with a deadline and a requirement to place a meaningful amount in one asset. A 66-unit building in a submarket with proven recent closings solves an identification problem that four small buildings do not.

buyer_profiles.title: The Value-Add Operator Buying the Rent Gap
buyer_profiles.copy: An operator who underwrites the difference between in-place and market rent and has a plan for capturing it on turnover. For this buyer the vacant units are not a discount to negotiate, they are the part of the business plan that is already available on day one.

rent_control.conclusion: The property sits in the City of Santa Clarita, which has no local rent stabilization ordinance and no local just-cause ordinance. A 1972 building is therefore governed by the statewide Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482), which caps annual increases at 5% plus CPI to a 10% ceiling and permits a reset to market rent on voluntary turnover.

zoning.conclusion: The Los Angeles County Assessor records the parcel as a Multi-Family Residence, use code 0500 and design type 0530, five or more units at four stories or less, with 66 units built in 1972. Zoning is administered by the City of Santa Clarita, and the existing apartment use is the use of record.

development.conclusion: No development yield, density bonus, or entitlement outcome is relied upon in this valuation. The property is valued as an existing income-producing apartment building.

Newhall Terrace Apartments is a 66-unit apartment building at 24377 Newhall Avenue in Santa Clarita, built in 1972 on a 2.14 acre parcel and containing approximately 36,908 gross square feet across two stories.

The property is a single floor plan asset. All 66 units are one bedroom, one bath homes of approximately 550 square feet, which makes the rent roll unusually simple to underwrite and unusually simple to manage: one unit type, one turn cost, one market rent to solve for.

Rents in place average $1,583 per month. The market rent carried in the analysis is $1,950. Applied across all 66 units, that gap is roughly $290,000 of annual scheduled rent that the property is not currently collecting, and no entitlement, construction, or repositioning is required to reach it.

Because Santa Clarita has no local rent stabilization ordinance, the gap closes on turnover rather than through a capped annual increase. Seven units were vacant at the rent roll date, which means a portion of that repositioning is available to a buyer immediately rather than over a holding period.
Walking Distance to Metrolink in Old Town Newhall

The property sits on Newhall Avenue at the edge of Old Town Newhall. Newhall Metrolink Station is three tenths of a mile away, a six minute walk, putting a tenant on a one seat rail ride to Burbank, Glendale, and Union Station without a car. The Oaks Plaza is two tenths of a mile from the door and the Newhall Crossings retail and residential development is three tenths of a mile.
William S. Hart Regional Park is a twelve minute walk. College of the Canyons is 4.8 miles out and Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital, one of the valley's largest employers, is 1.9 miles away.

This is the walkable end of the Santa Clarita Valley, which is uncommon in a market built overwhelmingly around the car. For a building of 550 square foot one bedrooms, a tenant base that can live here without a second vehicle is not a soft amenity, it is what supports the rent.

Two stories, 66 units, approximately 36,908 gross square feet on a 93,152 square foot lot. The Los Angeles County Assessor records the property under APN 2830-017-015 as a Multi-Family Residence built in 1972, and the unit count, year built, building area, and lot size in this analysis all tie to that record.
Improvements sit across garden-style wings with on-site surface parking and on-site laundry facilities. Every unit has air conditioning and heating.
At 2.14 acres the parcel is generously sized for 66 units, roughly 31 units to the acre, with meaningful open and landscaped area rather than a building built to its lot lines.

The site is a single legal parcel assembled from lots 29, 30, 31 and 32 of Tract 1059 together with the adjoining vacated street, held in fee simple. It fronts Newhall Avenue between 9th Street and Chestnut Street.
Nearby leased and asking rents are shown as a market sensitivity for the one bedroom floor plan and are not represented as achieved subject rents.

The recommendation is built on current income rather than on the pro forma. Closed arm's-length sales in Newhall run from $176,607 to $209,091 per unit, and the only closed trade at comparable scale, a 65-unit building half a mile up the same street, allocated at $182,692 per unit inside a four-property portfolio transaction.

On a per unit basis the recommendation sits at the upper end of that closed range, and on income it does not. The one closed sale in the set carrying a confirmed cap rate traded at 5.42%, and the escrow half a mile away is at 5.31%. The recommended value prices this property in line with both while its gross rent multiplier stays below every income-supported comparable in the analysis.

Two things move this number more than the comparables do. The first is the rent gap: 23% of upside on a building with no local rent control is what justifies pricing at the top of the per unit range rather than the middle. The second is expense underwriting. Repairs and management are carried at underwritten figures rather than the amounts on the owner's most recent operating summary, and a buyer who underwrites to those actuals will arrive at a lower net operating income. The sensitivity table shows that case explicitly.

The property was originally developed with 1987 low-income housing tax credits. That allocation carried a fifteen-year compliance period and no extended-use covenant, since the thirty-year requirement arrived only for allocations after 1989, and the restrictions expired in 2002. Ownership confirms the property carries no rent restriction and no age restriction today. Third-party data services still display the historical allocation, which is a record of a 1987 program rather than a live covenant. It does explain the rent profile: rents were held down for fifteen years and were never reset to market afterward.

rent_control.conclusion: The property sits in the City of Santa Clarita, which has no local rent stabilization ordinance and no local just-cause ordinance. A 1972 building is therefore governed by the statewide Tenant Protection Act (AB 1482), which caps annual increases at 5% plus CPI to a 10% ceiling and permits a reset to market rent on voluntary turnover.

zoning.conclusion: The Los Angeles County Assessor records the parcel as a Multi-Family Residence, use code 0500 and design type 0530, five or more units at four stories or less, with 66 units built in 1972. Zoning is administered by the City of Santa Clarita, and the existing apartment use is the use of record.

development.conclusion: No development yield, density bonus, or entitlement outcome is relied upon in this valuation. The property is valued as an existing income-producing apartment building.

exceptions.description: CoStar tags the subject Market Segment Senior, Rent Type Affordable, Affordable Type Rent Restricted, Affordable Units 66. This traces to a real primary record: HUD LIHTC database entry CAA00000007, state ID CA-87-033, 24377 NEWHALL AVE, SANTA CLARITA, 66 total and 66 low-income units, tax credits allocated 1987. ZIP+4 91321-2726 and coordinates 34.3786 / -118.531778 match APN 2830-017-015. The property WAS a 1987 Low-Income Housing Tax Credit deal. The restrictions have since lapsed: a 1987 allocation carries a 15-year compliance period and no extended-use covenant, because the 30-year requirement added by OBRA 1989 does not reach pre-1990 allocations. Logan Ward confirmed directly with ownership on 2026-09-04 that there is no LIHTC restriction and no senior restriction on the property now, and that the restriction fell off in 2002. That is consistent with every other fact on file: the City of Santa Clarita affordable rental housing list does not include the property, the assessor records Exemption None with an individual owner, the September 2006 sale to individuals for $6,250,000 came just after a 1987 compliance period would have run out, and in-place rents spread from $1,425 to $1,880 rather than sitting on an AMI schedule. The property is therefore underwritten and marketed as unrestricted market-rate housing, and the HUD database entry is a historical allocation record rather than a live covenant.
exceptions.approval_note: Logan Ward, chat, 2026-09-04: confirmed with ownership that there is no LIHTC or senior restriction on the property now and that the restriction fell off in 2002.

exceptions.description: The City of Santa Clarita publishes no open zoning service for the parcel and the county portal carries only the reference SCSP. The zoning conclusion therefore rests on the assessor's recorded use, a Multi-Family Residence of 66 units built in 1972, and no development yield is relied upon anywhere in the valuation.
